claim: On a deliberately deceptive task, a plain objective can be no better than random selection, while novelty-driven search over a coarse behaviour space solves it almost every time. Hard maze: fitness 3/40, random 4/40, novelty 39/40.
schema_part: G/S: diversify before committing (restart and branch states)
agent_test: Build 20 problems where a greedy partial-credit signal is known to mislead (a tempting wrong sub-answer). Compare greedy refine-by-score against branch-by-different-approach at equal tokens; count solves. Mostly a boundary-mapping test: the maze is hand-built and Pugh uses the same maze family, so the two sources are not fully independent.

claim: Novelty has a boundary: when the behaviour space is unbounded, novelty search lost its edge (5/100 solved vs fitness 2/100, not significant). Novelty also does not polish solutions; the authors suggest combining it with objective search. Gap search: pure novelty also lost to plain ES on a non-deceptive humanoid task (p<0.05), and an adaptive reward-then-novelty hybrid fixed that (d13, d14); a fixed explore-then-exploit hand-off beat plain DDPG on deceptive and non-deceptive control tasks (d15).
schema_part: G (cap on exploration), O (switch from explore to exploit)
agent_test: Run explore-then-exploit against explore-only at equal tokens; add a hard cap on the number of distinct approaches. Check whether uncapped diversification wastes tokens.

claim: The behaviour descriptor must be aligned with success. An aligned descriptor (maze end point) beat fitness (p<0.001); an unaligned one (facing direction) was worse than fitness (p<0.05) and solved the symmetric gauntlet in only 2 of 20 runs. Kistemaker and Whiteson independently found that over-fine or irrelevant behaviour dimensions slow search (63,440 to 27,427 evals when over-discrimination was removed; 21 and 29 of 70 runs failed with 3 and 4 behaviour points).
schema_part: O (diversity axis choice), memory (archive keys)
agent_test: For one task family define the diversity axis three ways (goal-aligned: method class; unaligned: answer length or style; none). Compare solve rate at equal tokens. Prediction: aligned beats none beats unaligned.

claim: MAP-Elites (one best per cell of a user-chosen grid) beats an ordinary EA, novelty search with local competition, and random sampling on coverage and reliability. On the retina task it won all four criteria (p<1e-7, 20 runs); on soft robots it did NOT beat controls on best single solution (p>0.05) and was worse on precision (p<0.01).
schema_part: memory (archive of attempts keyed by descriptor)
agent_test: Compare best-single-answer accuracy and coverage of distinct valid approaches for archive-driven search against plain best-of-N at equal tokens. Expect a coverage gain and no best-answer gain.

claim: Adding an adaptive optimiser as the emitter inside a MAP-Elites archive beats plain MAP-Elites in quality and coverage on continuous problems. Hearthstone QD-score 63,295.6 vs 25,936.0 (MAP-Elites) vs 16,024.8 (CMA-ES); win rate 65.9% vs 45.2%. Sphere n=20 cells filled 90.3% (CMA-ME rd) vs 56.2% vs 3.5%.
schema_part: O (exploit operator inside a diversity archive)
agent_test: In an LLM archive loop compare random-parent mutation against improvement-guided parent choice (pick the cell where recent edits improved). Equal tokens.

claim: An LLM can replace the mutation operator in a QD loop because it makes several coupled code edits at once: on 4-Parity bug fixing, GP mutation success falls exponentially and is zero at five bugs while the 300M diff model degrades only at five. ELM filled most of 1,728 niches from one seed program. LMX (few-shot crossover) shows validity depends on model size and prompt order (over 50% swing from parent order).
schema_part: O (variation operator), G (order-robustness: shuffle parents)
agent_test: Test whether prompt-order permutations of the same parent set change validity; use a majority over 2-3 orderings at equal tokens against one ordering with more samples.

claim: LLM-judged diversity and quality can look better than they are. QDAIF beat all baselines on AI-judged QD score, but under human judgement it only tied a fixed few-shot prompt (0.772 vs 0.767 QD; quality rating 3.90 vs 4.13, lower). AI-human quality correlation breaks at the top of the scale (0.995-1), a sign of judge hacking. LLM judges also track humans worse when human ratings are close.
schema_part: G (do not trust a self-judge at the top of its scale), S (verify state)
agent_test: Run a QD loop with a self-judge and score outputs with an independent verifier or human sample. Report the judge-vs-verifier gap at equal tokens and compare against a strong fixed-prompt baseline.

claim: Reusing earlier archive entries as parents (stepping stones) and mutating across cells beat regenerating from scratch or staying inside one cell: Rainbow Teaming mean fitness 0.91, coverage 0.97, self-BLEU 0.50 vs 0.79, 0.90, 0.60 without stepping stones. Code-evolution ablations (CodeEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, LEVI) agree in direction, but all are authors' own systems with few seeds.
schema_part: memory (reuse of prior attempts), O (cross-cell recombine)
agent_test: Same task and token budget: parent drawn from an archive of earlier attempts against always starting from the original problem. Count solves and distinct valid methods.

claim: Embedding-based novelty rejection (drop proposals with cosine similarity above 0.95 to existing programs) improves sample efficiency in LLM code evolution; an extra LLM novelty judge adds only marginally. Large over-generated pools are full of duplicates: only about 5% (200 of 4,000) of seed ideas survived dedup at cosine 0.8.
schema_part: G (duplicate filter before spending tokens), S (candidate pool)
agent_test: Add a cheap embedding duplicate filter to a best-of-N pool; measure unique-approach count and solve rate at equal tokens, and record how many tokens duplicates consumed.

claim: Frontier LLMs sampled repeatedly give few distinct answers, and different models agree with each other (cross-model similarity 71-82%), so a mix of models is not a source of independent diversity. Temperature, paraphrase and a creativity system prompt help little; showing the model its previous answers and asking for a different one lifts diversity to about human level. Gap search: in Core War a 4-model ensemble gave more archive coverage than a same-model ensemble at equal calls (80.6% vs 59.0%, d06), so cross-model independence may differ for code search than for open-ended answers; in-context regeneration was only compared with other prompts, not with an archive loop (d05).
schema_part: O (diversify operator = condition on prior outputs), G (same-model samples are not independent)
agent_test: Compare n samples at temperature against n sequential generations that see prior answers, at equal tokens; measure distinct-approach count and solve rate.

claim: Island-structured evolutionary search over whole solutions with an evaluator beats Best-of-N and sequential revision (Mind Evolution, Gemini 1.5 Flash: TravelPlanner 95.6% vs 55.6% and 82.8%). The island split gave about 10 points on a hard subset at equal conversations (87.5% vs 77.4%). FunSearch and AlphaEvolve report new results with island or MAP-Elites databases, but the archive's own contribution is not isolated. Gap search: the Mind Evolution ablation table puts most of the gain on the critic step and evaluator feedback (success 46.1% rising to 95.6% as components are added), with islands about 10 points; no recombination-only ablation exists, and all of it needs a programmatic evaluator.
schema_part: S (multiple populations), O (select/recombine), memory
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of 4 islands x 5 against 1 island x 20 on a verifiable task (planning or code). Cleanest test; needs an automatic checker.

claim: Quality and diversity trade off in a controllable way: a parent-child similarity filter cost some success (ASR 0.92 vs 0.99) but roughly halved repetition (self-BLEU 0.42 vs 0.79); a stricter quality cutoff when distilling an archive gave higher-quality but less diverse data (95K at 80% vs 280K at 50%). Quality-only optimisation gave no diversity (LMX quality-only human QD 0.650).
schema_part: G (explicit quality/diversity dial), O
agent_test: Sweep a similarity threshold in a candidate filter at equal tokens; plot solve rate against distinct-approach count to find the knee.

claim: An LLM can serve as a model of interestingness or a descriptor labeller, but agreement with humans is moderate and tested only at small scale. OMNI filtering raised interesting tasks learned in Crafter from 9 (learning progress) to 14 of 15; QDAIF AI-human diversity-label agreement was 0.833 vs human-human 0.800 in a small study. b27 and c27 are the same paper.
schema_part: O (descriptor assignment by the model), G (check label noise)
agent_test: Have the model label its own attempts by approach class; compare with a second-pass label by a separate call or a human on 50 items; report agreement and whether bad labels hurt archive coverage.

claim: Showing the whole archive (solutions with fitness and descriptors) in the prompt can match or beat MAP-Elites with mutation on synthetic tasks, but coverage was about equal because coverage is easy; a fitness-only prompt finds the best solution but poor coverage.
schema_part: memory (archive in context)
agent_test: Prompt template ablation on the agent: fitness only vs fitness plus descriptor vs parameters only; equal tokens.

claim: A diversity archive built before a failure can be a prior for fast adaptation after it: a 13,000-gait hexapod map let the robot recover in about 8 trials and 66 s median after damage (0.21 vs 0.04 m/s with a leg missing), but the map cost about two weeks of compute.
schema_part: memory (precomputed strategy library), O (fallback on failure)
agent_test: Keep a small library of distinct strategies per problem type and try the next when a check fails; compare with re-sampling at equal tokens.

claim: Whether QD archives help LLM agents on reasoning tasks (not code, maths constructions, red-teaming or creative writing) is untested. Published ablations are all in those other domains. Gap search: the nearest ARC work (Land 2026) diversifies by reasoning channel and judges holistically (+7 tasks over majority vote), but has no archive and no equal-token best-of-N control; the author lists those ablations as not run (d07). Still untested.
schema_part: none (scope limit)
agent_test: Run the K11 and K09 tests on the project's ARC and BrainTeaser items.

claim: Without a programmatic verifier, picking among many diverse attempts hits a ceiling, and optimising against a model judge past an optimum lowers true quality. MATH, Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% to 98.44% from 100 to 10,000 samples while majority vote or reward-model selection moved only 40.50% to 41.41%. A learned process reward model can be fooled: 44 strict exploits under mean pooling vs 1 under minimum readout (max gain 0.294).
schema_part: G (judge not trusted alone), O (verify with a hard check)
agent_test: Replace the model judge in one loop with a held-out test or a min-style check; compare solved count at equal tokens and the AI-vs-true quality gap. Sources are on maths and learned reward models, not on QDAIF-style diversity scoring.

claim: Corrected Rainbow Teaming vs PAIR numbers (JailbreakBench, 100 behaviours): Llama Guard 66 jailbreaks across 41 behaviours vs 14 across 11 for PAIR with the same mutator LLM; JBB classifier 8/7 vs 1/1; self-BLEU 0.51 vs 0.74. PAIR was given 2,000 prompts (20 streams), Rainbow Teaming 1,000, so the QD side had half the prompts. No PAIR restarts were run.
schema_part: memory (archive of distinct attempts)
agent_test: Re-run with a restart-enabled single-stream baseline at the same prompt budget before treating the gap as pure QD effect.

claim: In an LLM QD loop the judge is the main cost: Rainbow Teaming uses 2 mutator, 1 target and 4 judge calls per iteration (judge 57% of calls), 14,000 batched calls per 2,000 iterations, about two days on 128-256 A100s. Embedding dedup is reported as cheap and an extra LLM novelty judge added only marginal gain (ShinkaEvolve). No source reports token or wall-clock shares for descriptor labelling alone.
schema_part: budget (G: count scoring tokens)
agent_test: Instrument a prototype loop to log tokens per role (generate, label, judge, embed) and report shares; budget judge tokens inside the matched-token comparison.

claim: Explore-then-exploit hybrids have measured switch rules, but only in control tasks. NSRA-ES weights reward over novelty, cuts the reward weight by 0.05 after 50 generations without a new best, and raises it when progress resumes; it beat ES on 8/12 Atari games and tied it on a non-deceptive humanoid task. Changing the weight every 50 vs every 10 generations decided whether it escaped the Seaquest trap. GEP-PG hands a fixed exploration phase to DDPG and was stable over 100-600 exploration episodes.
schema_part: O (switch explore to exploit), G (stagnation counter)
agent_test: Implement 'no improvement in k attempts, force a different method' and sweep k (for example 2, 4, 8) at equal tokens on a deceptive subset; there is no LLM measurement yet.

claim: Plain novelty is not free and is not the only fix for deception. Pure novelty lost to ES on a non-deceptive humanoid task (p<0.05) and in many Atari games; lexicase selection over many sub-objectives beat MAP-Elites on deceptive maze and tour domains (10 replicates) without any explicit diversity measure. Real deceptive cases found: 5 of 12 Atari games (ES stuck), the rest were not deceptive.
schema_part: G (do not diversify by default), O (score on separate sub-checks)
agent_test: Compare an archive loop with a loop that scores each candidate per test case and selects on the per-case profile (lexicase-style) at equal tokens.

claim: The closest ARC result to a diversity-first loop: independent candidates across text, image and code channels, then a judge that reads all traces, solved 76.1% (public) and 72.9% (semi-private, $38.99 per task); the judge beat majority vote by net +7 tasks, all minority-answer recoveries. The author did not run independent-vs-sequential, candidate-scaling or modality ablations, and gives no confidence intervals.
schema_part: S (parallel attempts by method), O (judge over traces)
agent_test: Run N independent method-diverse attempts against N sequential refinements at equal tokens on ARC items; compare majority vote, judge, and judge with a duplicate filter.

claim: Descriptor choice needs a smooth map from small edits to descriptor changes and a link to success; this is shown in robot control only. Judge agreement with humans for a classifier-style label is 78-83% (Rainbow Teaming, 100 pairs), the same as human-human 83%. Nothing measures labeller agreement for reasoning-method descriptors.
schema_part: descriptor design (method class, first step)
agent_test: Label 100 reasoning attempts by method class with two labellers (two model calls with different prompts, plus a human sample); report agreement and the correlation of the class with success.
